title: Model-aware autoscaler and traffic slicing for Dedicated pools (PRD sketch)
body:
Purpose:
This sketch proposes a model-aware autoscaling and traffic-slicing system for Dedicated capacity that treats requests not just as tokens-per-second load but as structured signals (model type, sequence-length distribution, KV-cache re-use, latency-sensitive vs batch). The goal is to reduce cost and tail latency for tenants while preserving stronger isolation guarantees when needed.

Problem statement / motivation:
- Current autoscalers treat incoming RPS or token rate as a single-dimensional signal. That conflates cheap short-context requests (e.g., embeddings, small prompts) with expensive long-generation chat sessions.
- Tenants with mixed workloads get unpredictable unit costs and noisy interference: a spike of long-context generations from tenant A can create queuing that hurts latency for tenant B on the same pool.
- Burst lanes today are coarse: either allow burst or deny based on static credits. We need more fine-grained shaping that accounts for model cost profile and request heterogeneity.

High level goals (measurable):
- Reduce cross-tenant P99 latency impact from long-context spikes by 50% in mixed-workload pools.
- Lower average token-cost uplift from conservative autoscale padding by 20% (compared to current headroom policy) via smarter per-class capacity reservations.
- Provide graceful fallbacks (model or quantization) per-tenant with predictable SLO degradation windows.

Non-goals:
- This PRD does not propose changes to billing primitives or per-token pricing.
- Not addressing physical GPU packing or per-instance kernel tuning; this sits above runtime kernel selection.

Key ideas / components:
1) Request-classification pipeline (fast, deterministic):
   - Classify each request into a small set of runtime classes: SHORT-CHAT, LONG-STREAM, EMBEDDING, RERANK/BATCH, and KV-HIT (prefix-hit-heavy).
   - Classification uses three cheap headers/signals: model-id, requested-max-tokens, presence-of-kv-cache-key, and tenant-declared qos_hint (optional).
   - This classification is computed in the front proxy and attached as routing metadata.

2) Model cost profiles registry (per-model fingerprint):
   - Lightweight profile entries: avg-peak-flops-est, median-token-latency, KV-cache-benefit, memory-footprint-range.

(Note: this is a flat string field appended to stay within single-level JSON)
   - Profiles are periodically updated by an offline measurement job and exposed to autoscaler.

3) Multi-dimensional autoscaler (controller):
   - Instead of a single target utilization number, autoscaler reasons about capacity per request-class and per-model-family.
   - Maintain soft capacity reservations: for example, reserve X vGPU-equivalents for LONG-STREAM class and Y for EMBEDDINGS. Reservations are elastic: when unused, capacity flows to opportunistic pool.
   - Capacity represented in logical units (vGPU-equivalents) calculated from model cost profiles and current batch efficiency numbers.

4) Traffic slicing and soft isolation gates:
   - At the serving layer, requests are placed into per-tenant per-class queues with configurable QOS weights and max concurrency.
   - Gate rules: when headroom is low, allow short cheap classes to continue (fast-lane) while preempting or throttling long-running stream classes.
   - Tenant-level feature: an isolation flag (hard|soft|none) controls fallback behavior. Hard isolation prohibits stealing of reserved units; soft allows borrowing with compensation metrics.

5) Fallbacks and graceful degradation policies:
   - Policy table per-tenant: fallbacks ordered by cost/latency (e.g., smaller model -> quantized variant -> shorter max_tokens). Each fallback has an impact estimate.
   - Autoscaler can proactively suggest or enact fallbacks when it predicts a capacity deficit for the next N minutes.

6) Predictive short-term controller:
   - Sliding-window predictor estimates class-level demand over a 1–5 minute horizon using lightweight time-series features (EWMA + fast Fourier features for periodic signals).
   - If predicted demand > available capacity + buffer, trigger either scale-up or selective gating/fallbacks depending on latency-cost tradeoff.

Operational primitives and APIs:
- PoolConfig schema (new fields):
   - class_reservations: mapping of class -> logical_units (stringified in config UI)
body_continued_2:
- isolation_mode: hard|soft|none
   - fallback_priority_list: CSV of fallback ids
   - preempt_policy: oldest_stream|lowest-qos|random

- Admin endpoints: simulateTrafficSlice(), estimateHeadroom(tenant, forecast_minutes), forceFallback(tenant, fallback_id)

Metrics / SLOs to drive decisions:
- Per-class concurrency, tokens/sec, avg/kth-percentile latencies
- Reservation utilization ratio (reserved-used / reserved) per-class
- Opportunity-usage (percent of reserved units currently borrowed by opportunistic jobs)
- Cost delta when autoscaler switches to gating vs scale-up (for postmortem)
- Tenant-level degradation windows (time percent in fallback state)

Rollout plan (phases):
- Phase 0 (canary): implement request-classification and expose model profiles. Route 5% of small dedicated pools through classification to validate signal quality (2 weeks).
- Phase 1 (closed beta): implement traffic slicing + soft isolation gates for a handful of strategic tenants (4–6 weeks). Monitor latency impact and false-positive throttles.
- Phase 2 (autoscale integration): wire predictive controller to autoscaler with per-class reservations enabled, start with simulation mode then active control (6–8 weeks).
- Phase 3 (optimize): refine reservation sizing, fallback heuristics, and surface tenant-facing controls in Console (3–4 weeks).

Safety and guardrails:
- Always provide a global fail-open: if controller health is unknown, revert to current autoscaler behavior (single-dim autoscale).
- Fallbacks must be reversible within a request if possible (e.g., return a suggested fallback header to client rather than silently degrading for new sessions).
- All preemptions logged with tenant impact tag for billing/ops review.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How should we price or credit borrowed capacity in soft-isolation mode? (ops + finance decision)
- Should tenants be able to ship their own per-request QOS hints? Risk of misuse by noisy tenants.
- Complexity vs benefit: does per-class reservation materially reduce tail latency compared to improving queueing primitives and batch scheduling? Need offline simulations.

Engineering notes / implementation hints:
- Leverage existing front-proxy headers to carry classification metadata; keep classifier deterministic and cheap (no ML model in hot path).
- Autoscaler changes live in orchestration layer; add a lightweight reservations cache in Redis for fast lookup by routers.
- Use existing model profiling pipeline (ENG-4217) to seed initial cost profiles; add a nightly job that computes per-model tokens-per-second benchmarks at a few sequence lengths.

Risks and mitigations:
- Misclassification leading to poor routing: mitigate by conservative defaults and fallback to single-dim mode for unknown model-ids.
- Increased operational complexity: start selective beta and build tooling to visualize per-class utilization and reservation flows in Console.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Production beta tenants report no more than 10% increase in error/reject rate vs baseline during two-week test windows.
- Observed P99 latency for non-stream short-class requests improves by target amount in mixed pools.
- Autoscaler cost uplift reduced by target compared to baseline in simulated workloads.

Next steps / immediate action items:
- Sync with applied-ml to define minimal model profile fields and measurement harness (owner: Leo, due 2025-01-20).
- Build classification header spec and update front-proxy (owner: Diego, due 2025-01-28).
- Start a replay simulation: run historical traffic through class-based autoscaling simulator to estimate wins/losses (owner: Priya, due 2025-02-07).

Notes to reviewers:
- Looking for feedback on the reservation sizing heuristic and whether hard isolation should be tenant-configurable at signup. Also interested in ideas for simple compensation/crediting models for soft-borrow scenarios.
